venue_now: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p. 1 footer: '39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks'); the fetched text is arXiv:2509.16204v2, 6 Nov 2025 (p. 1)
what_it_is: EngDesign evaluates LLMs on open-ended engineering design rather than question answering: 101 design tasks across nine domains (operating systems, computer architecture, control, mechanical systems, structures, digital hardware, analog IC, robotics, signal processing), each with a task description, a rubric totalling 100 points with partial credit, an automated evaluation pipeline and a validated reference design (pp. 2-5). Tasks were proposed by graduate students and researchers, pre-tested with o4-mini and passed two review rounds, the second by faculty domain experts; 101 of 186 proposals were kept (pp. 6, 28). The model returns a structured design (parameters, netlists, code), which task-specific scripts check with domain simulators such as SPICE, MATLAB and finite element analysis, returning pass/fail, a 0-100 score and a log (pp. 2, 4-6). Twelve LLMs are evaluated over three trials per task (p. 7).
domain: engineering design: operating system, computer architecture, control, mechanical systems, structural, digital hardware, analog integrated circuit, robotics and signal processing design (pp. 2, 5)
size: 101 tasks with 473 gradable rubric items; 67 open-source tasks (EngDesign-Open) and 34 that need MATLAB or Cadence; 23 tasks include images (pp. 3, 5). 12 LLMs (p. 7)
source_of_items: expert-written: proposed by graduate students and researchers 'drawing on open-source resources and their domain knowledge' (p. 6), with university course materials among the references (p. 12); 186 proposals from more than 40 contributors, 101 accepted (p. 28)
has_gold_traces: no: each task has a validated reference design that meets all requirements (p. 5), not a reasoning trace. The model is asked for a step-by-step 'reasoning' field, but only the design fields are parsed and scored (pp. 6, 30)
evaluation: simulation-based functional verification of the final design: task-specific scripts run domain simulators and return a binary pass/fail, a 0-100 rubric score with partial credit and an evaluation log (pp. 5-6); reported as average pass rate, average score and 'reasoning robustness', the tasks passed in all three trials over those passed in at least one (pp. 7, 30-31). Failures of three models were annotated by hand into error types (pp. 9-10), outside the scoring
human_validation: An LLM pre-test, then two review rounds, the second by faculty experts in each domain (p. 6); every reference design verified to meet all requirements (pp. 5-6); evaluation scripts written by people (p. 2). No inter-reviewer agreement and no check of the scoring scripts against human grading is reported

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025), while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' S-E3 (L199-205, closing): 'Evidently, existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning required for engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-E2: 'design generation' is accurate. Models must 'generate functional, objective-oriented engineering designs' (p. 1), such as controllers, structures, circuits and SSD configurations (pp. 2, 4). 'Tangential skill' is the May paper's framing: EngDesign presents design as the core of engineering practice (p. 2), and its tasks require domain knowledge, constraint reasoning and calculation (pp. 2, 9-10). S-E3 fits loosely: EngDesign explicitly replaces 'static answer checking' with 'simulation-driven functional verification' and partial credit (pp. 1-3, Figure 1), so 'outcome matching' is the wrong name for its scoring, though, like outcome matching, it scores only the final design and not the reasoning (pp. 6, 30). The gist, that it does not evaluate EngTrace's kind of step-by-step calculation, is right.

suggested_wording: EngDesign (Guo et al., 2025b) evaluates design rather than calculation: models propose designs for 101 expert-reviewed tasks across nine domains, and task-specific simulation pipelines score the designs' performance with partial credit, without examining the reasoning that produced them.
facts_to_cite: 101 design tasks across nine engineering domains, with 473 gradable rubric items (pp. 3, 5).
Each task has a description, a 100-point rubric with partial credit, an automated evaluation pipeline and a validated reference design (p. 5).
Designs are evaluated with domain-specific simulators (e.g., SPICE, the MATLAB Control System Toolbox, finite element analysis), which return pass/fail, a 0-100 score and a log (pp. 2, 5-6).
Tasks were contributed by graduate students and researchers and reviewed in two rounds, the second by faculty domain experts; 101 of 186 proposals were accepted (pp. 6, 28).
No model exceeds a 35% pass rate; o3 is best at 34.38%, and every model scores 0% on analog IC design (p. 7).
With iterative feedback, o3 approaches a 60% pass rate after ten iterations on a 71-task subset (p. 9).
Published in the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p. 1).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: a multi-discipline engineering domain (its control, structural, mechanical and signal-processing tasks overlap EngTrace's branches); expert-reviewed items with reference solutions (pp. 5-6); a deterministic, executable checker rather than an LLM judge (pp. 5-6); repeated trials per task (p. 7), comparable to EngTrace's decoding repeats. Lacks: generated instances (101 static tasks); gold reasoning traces (reference designs only, p. 5); step-level evaluation (the reasoning field is not scored, pp. 6, 30); contamination measures (none); validation of the checker against expert judgement with agreement statistics (none reported). Its tasks are open-ended, with non-unique solutions (p. 5), unlike EngTrace's single-answer calculation templates.
notes: Confidence is medium only for the verdict label: S-E2 alone is accurate, and 'imprecise' rests on 'tangential' and on S-E3's 'outcome matching'; the facts are not in doubt. The paper calls itself EngDesign, a name the May text never uses (it cites only 'Guo et al., 2025b'). Five of its authors (Xingang Guo, Huan Zhang, Lianhui Qin, Yanfeng Ouyang, Bin Hu) are also authors of TransportBench (Syed et al., 2024; author list in zhou2025engibench p. 11), which the May paper cites among the siloed benchmarks. A revised text could call design 'complementary' to EngTrace's calculation-style reasoning rather than 'tangential'.
